background.definition: Septic arthritis is an inflammatory response of one or more joints to a bacterial infection within the joint space.

list.listitem: 5.7 to 9 per 100,000 person years.
Two to 10 per 100,000 in the general population.
Twenty eight to 30 per 100,000 in patients with rheumatoid arthritis.
Staphylococcus aureus is the most common pathogen in native and prosthetic joint infections.
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is becoming more common, especially in patient’s with chronic illness, older age, and health care exposure.
Streptococcus pyogenes and Streptococcus pneumoniae are the second most common Gram-positive aerobic infections.
Gram-negative bacilli are common causes in the elderly and in IV drug users.
Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the most common pathogen among young, sexually active US adults.

Most cases are a consequence of occult bacteremia from skin and mucous membrane sources. Pneumonia, pyelonephritis, and skin infections serve as common extra-articular sites of infection causing bacteremic articular seeding.
The synovium is highly vascular and lacks a basement membrane, making it vulnerable to bacteremic seeding. Joint damage results from bacterial invasion, host inflammation, and tissue ischemia.

Bacterial enzymes and toxins are directly injurious to cartilage; the cartilage suffers damage as host neutrophils release reactive oxygen species and lysosomal enzymes. As the pressure increases within the joint, the synovial blood flow is compromised, resulting in cartilage anoxia.
Immunocompromised patients with joint prostheses undergoing dental procedures should receive chemoprophylaxis. C

Placing the synovial fluid sample into an aerobic blood culture media can increase the culture yield. B

list.listitem: The classic presentation of septic arthritis is an acutely swollen, tender, and hot joint with limited range of motion. Although fever and chills are common, fever is absent in 43% of patients with septic arthritis (sensitivity 57%, 95% CI, 52-62).
No studies to date have assessed the sensitivity and specificity of examination findings such as tenderness, swelling, and range of motion.

In the majority of cases, septic arthritis is monoarticular and involves a large peripheral joint; 10% of cases are polyarticular. The knee is involved in more than 50% of cases, followed by the hip (15%), ankle (9%), elbow (8%), wrist (6%), and shoulder (5%).

When differentiating septic arthritis from transient synovitis of the hip in children, the following four criteria are useful: history of fever, unable to weight-bear, ESR >40 mm/h, and WBC >12,000. If all four criteria are present, there is a 99.6% chance that the patient has a septic hip.

The cornerstone for diagnosis of septic arthritis includes arthrocentesis and synovial fluid analysis. The gold standard of diagnosis includes bacterial identification by synovial fluid analysis with Gram’s stain and culture.

The sensitivity of Gram stain ranges from 29% to 50%; culture sensitivity may be only as high as 82%. Progressively high rsynovial WBC counts increase the likelihood of septic arthritis: >25,000/uL: LR 2.9; >50,000/uL: LR 7.7; and >100,000/uL: LR 28. Greater than 90% polymorphonuclear leukocytes also increased the likelihood of septic arthritis (LR+ 3.4).

Blood cultures are positive in approximately half of the cases and should be obtained in all patients with suspected septic arthritis. Using aerobic blood culture bottles to culture synovial fluid increases the yield.
WBC, ESR, and CRP are commonly elevated but are nonspecific findings. They are somewhat helpful when normal in ruling out infection but are not helpful when infection is present.
In patients status post knee arthroplasty, synovial fluid cell counts and cloudy appearance help rule in the diagnosis.
Suspect septic arthritis in a patient with fever and a painful swollen joint.
Perform arthrocentesis and synovial fluid analysis and base treatment on the results.

Four criteria can differentiate septic arthritis from transient synovitis of the hip in children: history of fever, inability to bear weight, ESR >40 mm/h, and WBC >12,000. If all four criteria are present, there is a 99.6% chance that the patient has a septic hip.
Treatment of septic arthritis requires parenteral broad-spectrum antibiotics and surgical drainage. C
Coverage of gonorrhea, MRSA, Gram negatives, and pseudomonas should be considered in high-risk populations. C
Dexamethasone reduces the risk of joint disability in children. B

If the risk of MRSA and gonorrhea are low, begin therapy with a second- or third-generation cephalosporin until culture and sensitivity results are available. Use clindamycin in penicillin allergic patients.

Patients at increased risk for MRSA, such as from hemodialysis, DM, recent nursing home admission, or recent or current hospitalization, should be empirically treated with vancomycin plus a second- or third-generation cephalosporin.
IV drug users should be covered with vancomycin plus an antipseudomonas agent.
Critically ill patients should be started on a combination of vancomycin plus second- or third-generation cephalosporin.

Young, sexually active patients with signs and symptoms consistent with disseminated gonorrhea should be treated with ceftriaxone 1 g IV or IM daily for a minimum of 3 days plus empiric coverage for chlamydia.
Giving dexamethasone to children for 4 days prevents disability from septic arthritis; studies have not been done on adults.
In combination with antibiotics, the successful treatment of septic arthritis requires the removal of pus.
No studies show superiority of surgical drainage over arthrocentesis.
Joints with acute infection should be rested during initial workup and treatment.
Even though the research is limited, continuous passive motion devices are often used to decrease adhesions, improve cartilage nutrition, and enhance clearance of purulent exudates.
No studies exist to provide guidance on the optimal duration of antibiotic therapy. Conventionally they are given parenterally for up to 2 weeks or until signs improve, and then orally for 4 weeks.

Septic arthritis of cartilaginous joints (eg, the sacroiliac and sternoclavicular joints) is recommended to be treated with 4 to 6 weeks of parenteral antibiotics because of the high rates of osteomyelitis.

A randomized trial found that oral antibiotics started within 7 days of surgery or (if no surgery) the start of antibiotic therapy for bone and joint infections was noninferior to 6 weeks of intravenous antibiotics in terms of treatment failure and overall quality of life at 1 year.
About half of the patients in a series of 121 adults and 33 children had a poor joint outcome (defined as need for amputation, arthrodesis, prosthetic surgery, or severe functional deterioration). B
Adverse prognostic indicators include advanced age, preexisting joint pathology, and an infected joint containing synthetic material. B
Despite advances in antibiotics and methods of joint drainage, mortality rates continue to range from 10% to 15%. B
The elderly are more prone to Gram-negative infections because of preexisting comorbidities such as rheumatoid arthritis and diabetes mellitus.
Knee and hip involvement accounts for most septic joint infections in children.
Staph and strep bacteria are responsible for most infections; community-acquired MRSA is becoming a more common pathogen.
